stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Ines, a visiting birdwatcher, has just told her uncle Tomas that the swallows nesting in his barn are a nuisance and should be driven off.

TOMAS: A nuisance? Each of those birds eats hundreds of flies a day. Before they came, my cows were tormented from June to September. Drive the swallows off, and the flies will be back before summer ends. I would sooner lose the barn roof than lose those birds.
choices: Ines argues that the swallows in the barn are a nuisance and should be removed.
Tomas argues that the swallows are valuable because they keep flies away from his cows.
Tomas worries that the swallows nesting in the barn will soon damage its roof.
Tomas claims that swallows eat more flies than any other bird in the region.
explanation: The introduction tells you Tomas is answering Ines's complaint. In plain English, his lines say the swallows eat the flies that used to bother his cows, and the flies will come back if the birds leave. His last line, which says he would rather lose the roof than the birds, sums up that view: the swallows are worth keeping.

A.why: You summarized the other character. The introduction gives Ines's view, but the question is about Tomas's speech, and he argues against her.

C.why: You read 'I would sooner lose the barn roof' literally. Tomas isn't predicting damage. He is saying how much more he values the birds than the roof.

D.why: Tomas says each swallow eats hundreds of flies, but he never compares swallows with other birds. You added a claim the text doesn't make.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in an English weaving town in 1830. A merchant has just told Hannah, a hand-loom weaver, that the new power looms will soon put her out of work.

HANNAH: Thy machines may weave faster, I grant thee. But can they make a cloth that holds its pattern after twenty washings? Ask the ladies who buy from me whether they would trade my linen for thine. Speed is a fine thing, sir, but it is not the same as quality.
choices: Hannah accepts that power looms will soon make hand weaving an outdated trade.
Hannah is unsure whether machine-made cloth keeps its pattern after many washings.
Hannah argues that her handwoven cloth is better made, even if machines are faster.
Hannah explains that her customers are wealthy women who buy linen from her.
explanation: Rewrite Hannah's lines in plain English: 'Your machines may be faster, I'll admit. But their cloth doesn't last the way mine does, and my customers know it. Being fast isn't the same as being good.' She grants the merchant's point about speed and then argues for the quality of her own work.

A.why: This is the merchant's claim from the introduction. Hannah grants only that the machines are faster. She doesn't agree that her trade is finished.

B.why: You took a rhetorical question literally. 'Can they make a cloth that holds its pattern?' isn't a real question. Hannah means that they can't.

D.why: Hannah mentions her customers only to support her point about quality. You picked a passing detail instead of the claim it supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. A student has just called the speech of a coastal fishing village "bad English." Her professor responds.

"Bad? Listen to how the fishermen say 'I be mending' for work they do every day and 'I'm mending' for a single job. That is not carelessness, my dear. It marks a difference standard English cannot show in so few words. Their grammar is not broken; it is simply different from ours."
choices: The professor argues that the village speech follows consistent rules of its own.
The student argues that the village speech is a careless form of standard English.
The professor argues that standard English is less expressive than any dialect.
The professor notes that the fishermen mostly discuss mending their nets and boats.
explanation: The professor rejects the word 'bad' and gives an example: the fishermen use 'I be' and 'I'm' to mark two different meanings. His conclusion is in the last line: their grammar 'is not broken; it is simply different.' The dialect has its own system.

B.why: This is the student's view from the introduction, and it's the view the professor is arguing against. You matched the wrong speaker.

C.why: The professor says standard English can't make this one distinction as briefly. He never claims it is less expressive than every dialect.

D.why: 'Mending' appears only in the professor's example. You picked a detail from the illustration instead of the point it illustrates.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Two researchers are diving above a reef. Leo, a new assistant, has just surfaced to report that the coral below has turned white and must be dead.

DR. OKAFOR: White, yes, but not dead. Coral turns pale when warm water forces out the algae living inside it. If the water cools within a few weeks, those algae can return. Dead coral is soon covered with seaweed. Tell me, did you see any seaweed down there?
choices: Dr. Okafor argues that the white coral is dead and can no longer recover.
Dr. Okafor argues that the white coral is weakened but may still recover.
Dr. Okafor argues that the coral will certainly recover once the water cools.
Dr. Okafor is unsure whether any seaweed is growing on the reef below them.
explanation: Dr. Okafor's first words, 'White, yes, but not dead,' state her point. She explains that warm water has pushed the algae out of the coral and that they 'can return' if the water cools. Her closing question suggests Leo saw no seaweed, so the coral isn't dead yet.

A.why: This is Leo's view from the introduction, and Dr. Okafor corrects it. You took the other character's claim for hers.

C.why: You missed the hedges. Dr. Okafor says the algae 'can' return 'if' the water cools within weeks. That is a possibility, not a promise.

D.why: You took a rhetorical question literally. Dr. Okafor isn't asking because she doesn't know. She's leading Leo to see that there is no seaweed.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Ruth, a patient trying to improve her diet, has just proudly told her dietitian that she has cut every bit of fat from her meals.

DIETITIAN: Every bit? Then how is your body to absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K, which dissolve only in fat? The goal was never to eat no fat, Ruth. It was to choose it well: olive oil, nuts, and fish rather than fried food and pastry.
choices: The dietitian praises Ruth for removing all fat from her daily meals.
The dietitian lists four vitamins that the body absorbs only with fat.
The dietitian advises Ruth to choose healthier fats, not to avoid all fat.
The dietitian wonders how the body is able to absorb certain vitamins.
explanation: The dietitian says it directly: 'The goal was never to eat no fat... It was to choose it well.' The point about vitamins explains why cutting all fat is a mistake, and the list of foods shows which fats to choose.

A.why: You took Ruth's pride from the introduction and gave it to the dietitian. The dietitian's 'Every bit?' questions Ruth's choice. It isn't praise.

B.why: This is true, but it covers only one sentence. The vitamins are the dietitian's reason, not her main point.

D.why: You took a rhetorical question literally. The dietitian knows how these vitamins are absorbed. Her question points out what Ruth's diet gets wrong.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Ida, a naturalist, speaks with Tom, a farmer who plans to drain a marsh on his land.

TOM: It's a bog. Nothing grows there that a man can sell.
IDA: Nothing you can sell, perhaps. But the herons nest there, the frogs breed there, and the spring floodwater that would reach your barn stops there first. Drain it, and you lose more than you gain.
choices: Tom explains that the marsh on his land produces nothing he is able to sell.
Ida argues that the marsh is worth keeping even though it yields nothing to sell.
Ida admits that the herons nesting in the marsh are the only reason to keep it.
Ida insists that every marsh in the region should be protected from farmers.
explanation: The intro tells you Tom wants to drain the marsh, so Ida's lines are a response to that plan. Put her speech in plain English: 'Fine, it makes no money, but it shelters wildlife and holds back floods that would hit your barn, so draining it costs you more than it earns.' That is the point the whole exchange builds toward, and B states it.

A.why: You summarised the other character's line. Tom does say this, but it is only the setup that Ida answers. The text as a whole does more than this, so the choice is too narrow.

C.why: You stopped reading after 'herons'. Ida lists herons, frogs and flood control together. Nothing in her speech makes the herons the only reason.

D.why: You stretched one marsh into every marsh in the region. Ida talks only about Tom's land and Tom's barn, and she never mentions protecting marshes in general.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in a nineteenth-century village. Hannah, a well-digger, answers a neighbor who asks why she will not dig a new well beside the tannery.

NEIGHBOR: The ground is soft there. Thou mayst dig it in half the time.
HANNAH: Soft ground drinks whatever is poured upon it. If the tannery's waste sinks into that soil, then the water we draw beneath it will carry the waste back to us. I'll dig farther off and gladly take the longer labor.
choices: The neighbor points out that soft ground near the tannery would be quicker to dig.
Hannah complains that digging any well in soft ground is too hard to be worth it.
Hannah explains that a well by the tannery would draw up water fouled by its waste.
Hannah claims that every well in the village is already fouled by the tannery.
explanation: Find the conditional in Hannah's speech: 'If the tannery's waste sinks into that soil, then the water we draw beneath it will carry the waste back to us.' In plain English, a well there would bring up polluted water, so she will dig somewhere else. C states that claim.

A.why: You picked the other character's point. 'Thou mayst dig it in half the time' belongs to the neighbor. It is only what Hannah is answering, and her answer is the main idea.

B.why: You read the old phrasing backwards. Hannah never says soft ground is hard to dig. She accepts the 'longer labor' of digging elsewhere, and she does it to avoid polluted water, not hard work.

D.why: You went beyond the text. Hannah warns about a new well beside the tannery. She says nothing about the wells the village already has.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Two fossil collectors examine a slab of stone holding the print of a fernlike leaf.

OWEN: A fern, plainly. Look at the fronds.
LUCIA: Look at the tips instead. Ferns carry spores beneath their fronds, but this leaf bears seeds along its edge. Whatever this plant was, it only dressed like a fern.
choices: Owen argues that the shape of its fronds shows the fossil plant to be a fern.
Lucia argues that the fossil plant was a fern because its leaf carries seeds.
Lucia argues that the fossil plant was not a fern despite resembling one.
Lucia argues that all ferns are descended from seed-bearing ancient plants.
explanation: Lucia answers Owen's claim by pointing to the seeds at the leaf's edge. Ferns use spores, not seeds. Her last line, 'it only dressed like a fern', means it looks like a fern but is not one. C states that point.

A.why: You picked the other character's view. Owen says it is a fern, but the scene exists so that Lucia can correct him. His line is the setup, not the main idea.

B.why: This choice starts on the right topic and then reverses Lucia's conclusion. She uses the seeds as proof that the plant is not a fern. Read every choice to the end.

D.why: You read in a broad claim about evolution that Lucia never makes. She is talking about one fossil, not about where ferns came from.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Rosa Ferrand, an engineer, speaks to a town councilman who wants a new bridge opened before winter.

COUNCILMAN: The steel is here. The crew is here. Why should we wait?
ROSA: Because the concrete in the piers has not yet cured. Put traffic on it now and it will hold—for a year, perhaps two. Wait a month, and it will hold for my grandchildren's grandchildren.
choices: The councilman asks Rosa why the steel and the crew arrived before the concrete.
Rosa warns that the bridge will fall the moment any traffic is allowed onto it.
Rosa argues that a short delay now will let the bridge last for generations.
Rosa argues that no bridge should ever be built during the winter months.
explanation: Rosa answers 'Why should we wait?' by contrasting two outcomes. Open now and the bridge lasts a year or two. Wait a month while the concrete cures and it lasts for generations. Her point is that the brief delay is worth it, which is C.

A.why: You took a rhetorical question literally. The councilman is not asking about delivery schedules. He means 'there is no reason to wait.' Either way, his line is the setup, not the main idea.

B.why: This exaggerates Rosa's warning until it contradicts her. She says the bridge would hold for a year or two, so she does not say it would fail at once.

D.why: You turned one bridge into a general rule. Rosa's objection is about this concrete not having cured, not about winter construction in general.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in the 1600s. A ship's captain questions Elias, a mapmaker, about a blank stretch of coast on his new chart.

CAPTAIN: Other charts fill that coast with towns and rivers. Why dost thou leave it bare?
ELIAS: Because no man I trust hath seen it. Were I to draw what I have only heard, then sailors would steer by my guesses. Better an empty page than a false one.
choices: The captain observes that other charts show more towns and rivers along that coast.
Elias admits that he left the coast blank because he ran out of time to finish it.
Elias claims that every other chart of that coast was drawn from false reports.
Elias argues that a blank coast is safer for sailors than one drawn from hearsay.
explanation: In plain English, Elias says: 'Nobody reliable has seen it. If I drew what I've only heard about, sailors would steer by my guesses. An empty page beats a wrong one.' His point is that leaving the coast blank protects sailors better than filling it with unverified features, which is D.

A.why: You summarised the other character's speech. The captain does say this, but only to prompt Elias's explanation, and that explanation is the point of the text.

B.why: You invented a reason Elias never gives. He leaves the coast blank on purpose because nobody reliable has seen it, not because he ran out of time.

C.why: You pushed Elias's caution too far. He says the coast is unverified, not that the other charts are definitely wrong.
